You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Non-farm payrolls cool down, rate hike expectations ease, storage tests AI narrative

TEXT:
Performance of Major Global Stock Indexes (USD denominated) and Valuations
Data source: Bloomberg
Key Takeaways
Last week, the US June non-farm payroll was significantly weaker than expected, with only 57,000 new jobs created, and revisions for the previous two months reducing the job count by 74,000. A decline in labor force participation also diminished the significance of the drop in the unemployment rate. The jobs data reduced the need for a near-term rate hike, resulting in a brief rotation of funds from high-growth AI sectors to rate-sensitive traditional industries; the Dow Jones hit a new record high, and there was a notable recovery in Greater China’s “old economy stocks.” In terms of AI, rising storage prices and Meta’s plan to rent out idle computing power have become focal points in the market, reflecting that AI capital spending is entering a new phase that emphasizes efficiency and returns. However, this does not mean the industry cycle has peaked; short-term stock price fluctuations are mainly driven by funding and sentiment.
In the medium-to-long term, as long as model vendors’ ARR continues to grow and AI Agent continues to deliver cost reductions and increased efficiency, the main line of AI CAPEX remains intact. This week’s focus will be Samsung’s Q2 earnings preview and SK Hynix’s ADR listing, which serve both as verification of the storage industry trend and as a stress test for the degree of crowdedness in the sector. However, whether the next phase of the rally will continue still depends on the US June CPI over the next two weeks, and whether TSMC and ASML’s financial reports confirm sustained demand for computing power and equipment orders.
Key Events to Watch This Week
US Market & Greater China Market
Last week, the US released the June non-farm payroll report, overall weaker than the previous “steady recovery” narrative of the job market. Non-farm payrolls increased by 57,000, about half of market expectations, and the previous two months were revised down by a total of 74,000. Labor force participation dropped from 61.8% to 61.5%, with the decrease in unemployment rate largely reflecting people leaving the workforce rather than a marked increase in hiring demand. By sector, the IT industry shrank by 9,000 jobs, and leisure/hospitality was down 61,000, the key drags behind the weak report. Meanwhile, average hourly earnings rose slightly to 3.5% year-on-year. High wage sectors such as IT, finance, and professional services continued to show wage resilience, indicating the job market is not universally weakening but instead shows a combination of “slower hiring, lower participation, and sticky wages.” For the market, this report reduced the necessity for near-term rate hikes, leading to a rotation of funds into rate-sensitive traditional sectors rather than AI industries. As a result, the Dow Jones set another record high, and Greater China’s “old economy stocks” experienced a notable rebound.
Data source: Bloomberg
Recently, there have been two main focuses in AI trading: rising storage prices and model vendors renting out idle computational power. Essentially, both point to increased constraints on AI capital expenditure efficiency, but do not mean the peak of the industry investment cycle. The surge in storage prices is reshaping cost and profit allocation, putting short-term pressure on consumer electronics and cloud vendors, and forcing the industry to place greater importance on investment returns. However, as new supply comes online in 2027–2028, the storage industry will likely shift from price-driven to volume-driven expansion, driving further demand for advanced storage and high-end packaging equipment. On the other hand, model vendors renting out idle computing power is more of a market mechanism for monetizing poorly utilized assets rather than simple excess supply. In the short-term, falling rental prices for previous-generation chips and pressure on small and medium data centers may impact sentiment. In the medium term, as long as model vendor ARR continues to grow and AI Agent continues to provide cost savings and efficiency gains, the AI CAPEX story remains intact—just moving into a new stage where models, hardware, applications, and cash flow are verified together.
Looking to this week, the focus remains on the AI storage sector. Samsung’s Q2 earnings preview and SK Hynix’s US ADR listing will be key events to test the strength of this storage—and broader semiconductor—cycle. We believe that it will be even more important this week to watch the pace of trading after the expected positives are realized, rather than the financial results themselves. The storage sector’s industry trends remain robust, but given extremely crowded positions and highly unified expectations, earnings releases and listing events may continue to offer windows for short-term profit-taking. Looking further ahead, the next catalyst or inflection point for the AI trade may wait until next week: at the macro level, the US June CPI data; at the industry level, TSMC and ASML’s earnings calls—whether they confirm sustained expansion in computing power demand, continued advanced process expansion, and strong semiconductor equipment orders—will be critical for the next phase of the AI rally.
